preamble: The shift of the voiceless dental fricative [θ] to the labiodental [f] is a context-free change driven by the acoustic similarity of the two weak, non-sibilant fricatives. It is best known as th-fronting in English dialects (Cockney, Estuary, AAVE, Bristol, Glasgow), but it has occurred independently in Semitic (Siirt Arabic, with incipient cases in Bahraini and Tunisian Arabic) and in Northern Athabaskan (Tulita Slavey). The reverse change f > θ is rare.

examples.note: Classic London th-fronting, recorded for 'low English' of London as early as 1787.
Th-fronting is especially frequent in word-final position.
In this Southern Anatolian dialect all original interdentals became labiodentals (*θ, *ð, *ðˤ > f, v, vˤ; vahab 'gold' < *ðahab).
Northern Athabaskan *θ, *ð became f, v in the Tulita district, at a stage when the language had no other labial obstruents, so the change was not a merger.

sources: Blevins, J. (2019). Deconstructing markedness in sound change typology: Notes on θ > f and f > θ. In Perspectives on Language Structure and Language Change (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 345), 107–122. John Benjamins. https://doi.org/10.1075/cilt.345.04ble
